newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weary cosmonaut plunges Mir into crisis.
newsitem.headline: Weary cosmonaut plunges Mir into crisis.

text.p: A weary cosmonaut aboard Russia's Mir space station mistakenly pulled out a vital computer cable on Thursday, plunging the crippled ship into its worst crisis since a near-fatal collision three weeks ago.

The three-man crew, whose commander developed a probably stress-induced heart problem this week, had to sit in their Soyuz escape capsule to communicate with Earth and were using flashlights to get around the darkened station.

"I should stress it is an especially unpleasant situation. It very much recalls the situation we were in after the crash," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow.

But the cosmonauts were in no immediate danger from the latest in this year's jinx-like series of Mir mishaps and had no plans to abandon ship, he said, even though light, heating and life-support systems were shut down on the main station.

The crew have stored oxygen for just five days, while the temperature and humidity will remain bearable for two or three days without power. That sets a clear time limit on re-starting Mir's life-support machines, including the oxygen generators.
Deputy mission director Viktor Blagov said he was confident, however, that the problems would be sorted.
It would be Thursday evening before Mission Control experts would be able to receive key data from Mir to give the crew advice. "We've always succeeded before," Blagov told reporters.

Meanwhile, the crew, who have been told to sleep in shifts, even had orders to go on preparing for next week's risky repair job to fix the electric cables damaged in the June 25 accident -- though a NASA official said a delay was now likely.

The tension was palpable at Mission Control in the biggest drama since last month's collision -- also possibly caused by a crew error -- which cut power by up to half and nearly cost the men their lives when one of Mir's modules was holed.
"Shut it down! Shut it down!" the duty mission controller barked into a microphone at Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev as the crew fought to save power after the overnight malfunction.
"This was purely human error," Solovyov said of the latest crisis. Officials have neither confirmed nor denied reports that a basic mistake by Tsibliyev caused the original collision.
Blagov said Mission Control had not asked which of the two Russians and one American aboard had pulled the computer plug during late night preparations for the planned cable repairs.
The crewman immediately put back the plug, connected to the station's computer system. But the damage was done.

The gyroscopic guidance system that keeps Mir's solar panels lined up to the Sun again malfunctioned -- it has been dogged by problems in the last three weeks -- driving the power supply down to the very minimum needed to keep the station running.

Commander Tsibliyev, 43, was pulled from the two-man repair team on Wednesday after developing an irregular heartbeat. NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, is due to step in to a spacesuit alongside flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39.

But they have just an hour of daylight during every two-hour orbit to continue preparations. And with other problems to contend with as well as signs of fatigue showing up in mistakes, the repair schedule seemed again in doubt.
"This will probably put a delay on the plans that we had," said Leroy Chiao, a NASA Shuttle astronaut working at Korolyov.
Officials have said that the job could be left for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7.

The collision was the worst accident in Mir's 11 years in space but by no means an isolated mishap, raising questions abroad over whether it should be ditched before a new international space station goes into action from next year.
Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they will not abandon the station.
But if conditions become untenable, the Mir crew will fly the Soyuz escape capsule home, condemning the 140-tonne complex to a premature end.
The British-born Foale's mother was keeping a stiff upper lip, however. "We are concerned," she said. "But not unduly."
